newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-UK inflation hits two-year high in July.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UK inflation hits two-year high in July.

text.p: The headline rate of inflation in Britain leapt to a near two-year high of 3.3 percent in July from 2.9 percent in June, official figures showed on Tuesday.

The Office for National Statistics said the underlying rate of inflation, which excludes volatile mortgage payments, jumped too. It reached 3.0 percent in July from 2.7 percent in June, well above the government's 2.5 percent.
But financial markets were unfazed. The FTSE-100 index of leading shares spurted 20 points higher to 5,052 and the pound was little changed at 2.94 marks.

Economists said the leap in July inflation was largely due to one-off effects, particularly a jump in petrol prices following duty increases in Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's first budget, and increased housing costs following a succession of recent interest rate rises.

"One factor that may prevent the market selling off too badly on this is that RPIY fell on the month," said Tom Rayner, economist at Societe Generale. The RPIY measure strips out mortgage interest payments and indirect taxes from the inflation equation, thus excluding any measures introduced in the July 2 budget.
That measure fell 0.2 percent between June and July and was just 2.2 percent higher than a year ago.

Inflation fears were also calmed by other components in the breakdown of Tuesday's figures. Household goods prices dropped 1.5 percent over the month while clothing and footwear prices tumbled 4.7 percent.

The Bank of England, which raised base rates for the fourth time in as many months last week, taking them to seven percent, has voiced concern at the inflationary effects of a flood of windfall payments from floating building societies -- 35 billion pounds in free shares at the last count.

Sales evidence shows that consumers have spent their windfalls on goods like washing machines and televisions, which come under the heading of household goods. But there is no evidence that retailers are pushing prices up in response.
"Clothing and footwear is very low, as is household goods inflation and those are components of retail sales where demand has been strongest of late," said Andrew Cates, UK economist at UBS.
"There is no evidence in these figures of any demand-led inflationary pressure."
